---
title: "3D Plotting"
description: "How pyorbiter chooses between a 2D matplotlib plot and an interactive 3D plotly figure, and how to make that choice yourself."
---

```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib
import pyorbiter as orb
```

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pyorbiter as orb
```

All simulations in `pyorbiter` run in full 3D. Every body always has `x`, `y`, and `z` coordinates. When all motion happens in the xy plane (`z = 0` and `vz = 0` for every body), [`plot_orbits()`](../reference/plot_orbits.qmd) draws a static 2D matplotlib plot. As soon as any body has a non-zero `z`, `plot_orbits()` switches to an interactive 3D plotly figure. No code changes are needed.

You can also force 3D rendering for planar data with `three_d=True`. This is useful if you want to rotate and zoom a flat system.

The 3D plots need plotly, which is an optional dependency. It comes with the `plotly` extra:

```bash
pip install "pyorbiter[plotly] @ git+https://github.com/DRosenman/pyorbiter.git"
```

## How the 2D/3D switch works

`plot_orbits()` checks whether any value in the `z` column of the simulation is non-zero. If there is any motion along z, or if you pass `three_d=True`, it hands off to [`plot_orbits_3d()`](../reference/plot_orbits_3d.qmd), which builds a plotly figure. Otherwise it draws the 2D matplotlib plot.

The `three_d` argument has three settings:

| `three_d` | Result |
|:--|:--|
| `None` (the default) | 3D only if some `z` value is non-zero |
| `True` | Always the 3D plotly figure |
| `False` | Always the 2D matplotlib plot, which shows the projection onto the xy plane |

The return value follows the plot. A 2D plot returns a matplotlib `Axes`. A 3D plot returns a plotly `Figure`.

If plotly is not installed, `plot_orbits()` issues a warning and falls back to the 2D plot, even for 3D data. Calling `plot_orbits_3d()` directly without plotly raises an `ImportError` instead.

[`plot_system()`](../reference/plot_system.qmd) and [`animate_system()`](../reference/animate_system.qmd) make the same choice in the same way, and take the same `three_d` argument. Their 3D counterparts are [`plot_system_3d()`](../reference/plot_system_3d.qmd) and [`animate_system_3d()`](../reference/animate_system_3d.qmd).

## A tilted lunar orbit

The Moon's real orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to the plane of Earth's orbit. You can approximate this by giving the Moon a small `vz` component:

```{python}
tilt = np.radians(5)

sim = (
    orb.create_system()
    .add_body("Earth", mass=orb.mass_earth)
    .add_body("Moon", mass=orb.mass_moon,
              x=orb.distance_earth_moon,
              vy=orb.speed_moon * np.cos(tilt),
              vz=orb.speed_moon * np.sin(tilt))
    .simulate(time_step=orb.seconds_per_hour, duration=orb.seconds_per_day * 28)
)

orb.plot_orbits(sim)
```

Because `vz` is non-zero, `plot_orbits()` detects 3D motion and returns an interactive plotly figure. Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, and hover over a line to see the body name and the time in days. The three axes share one scale, so the orbit keeps its true shape from any angle.

You can confirm what came back:

```{python}
fig = orb.plot_orbits(sim)
type(fig).__name__, len(fig.data)
```

The figure holds one `Scatter3d` line per body. It is an ordinary plotly figure, so `fig.update_layout()`, `fig.add_trace()`, and `fig.write_html("orbit.html")` all work on it. In a script, call `fig.show()` to open it in a browser.

The same tilted orbit can be set up without any trigonometry. [`add_body_keplerian()`](../reference/OrbitSystem.add_body_keplerian.qmd) takes the inclination `i` in degrees, and [`add_planet()`](../reference/OrbitSystem.add_planet.qmd) uses each body's real inclination unless you override it. See [Keplerian elements](keplerian-elements.qmd) for details.

## Forcing 3D for flat data

Even if your system is entirely planar, you can ask for the interactive 3D viewer:

```{python}
flat = (
    orb.create_system()
    .add_body("Earth", mass=orb.mass_earth)
    .add_body("Moon", mass=orb.mass_moon, x=orb.distance_earth_moon, vy=orb.speed_moon)
    .simulate(time_step=orb.seconds_per_hour, duration=orb.seconds_per_day * 28)
)

orb.plot_orbits(flat, three_d=True)
```

This gives you the same rotation and zoom controls, even though every `z` value is zero. Calling `orb.plot_orbits_3d(flat)` directly does the same thing.

## Forcing 2D for tilted data

The switch works in the other direction too. `three_d=False` draws the matplotlib plot for any data. For the tilted lunar orbit this is the view from straight above the xy plane, with the motion along z flattened out:

```{python}
orb.plot_orbits(sim, three_d=False);
```

Use this when you need a static image for a report, or when you want to draw on the result with matplotlib. The trailing semicolon only stops a notebook from printing the returned `Axes`.

## A snapshot in 3D

`plot_system()` shows where every body is at one time instead of the whole trajectories. With tilted data it returns the plotly figure from `plot_system_3d()`. Here is the system 7 days in, with the full orbits drawn faintly behind the markers:

```{python}
orb.plot_system(sim, time=7 * orb.seconds_per_day, trails=True)
```

`time` is in seconds from the start of the simulation, and the closest recorded time step is used. Hover over a marker to see the body name, the time in days, and the coordinates in meters.

Without `trails=True` the scene is fitted to the markers alone, so the view is tight around the bodies. With trails it covers the whole trajectories.

## An animation in 3D

`animate_system()` follows the same rule. For data with motion in z it returns the plotly figure from `animate_system_3d()`, which has Play and Pause buttons and a time slider labelled in days. You can rotate and zoom the scene while it plays.

```{python}
anim = orb.animate_system_3d(sim, fps=10, duration=4, trails=True)
anim
```

`fps` and `duration` set the number of frames. About `fps * duration` evenly spaced time steps are drawn, so this animation has 40 frames taken from the 673 recorded time steps:

```{python}
len(anim.frames), sim["time"].nunique()
```

`duration` is seconds of playback, not of simulated time.

The 3D animation is played by the browser. There is no image encoding, so the figure is built quickly even for many frames. The `path=` argument of `animate_system()`, which saves a GIF, applies only to the 2D matplotlib animation and is ignored in 3D. To save a 3D animation, write the figure to a standalone HTML file with `anim.write_html("orbit.html")`.

## Going further

The built-in 3D functions are meant to give a useful picture in one line. When you need something they do not cover, such as coloring a trajectory by speed, build the plotly figure yourself from the simulation DataFrame. [Custom visualization](custom-visualization.qmd) shows how.
